title: Man. Post. Cap. I: Placeus on ambiguity, Confession breach, consent dilemma; before Cap. II
pass_a_gloss: You subjoin the reason: for how did death then reign even unto those also who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, if this sin of Adam was not imputed to them? Fancy a child newly born or dying in the very womb of the mother: what is in him that can be called sin? will in him is void of all action, nor can he sin by his own will. He has in himself, you will say, seeds of sin—granted—but not yet sin properly, unless that sin of origin by which he sinned in Adam. Therefore his sin is to be sought not in him, or from himself, but in the first origin, that is, in the first parent: nor is that sin other than that voluntary disobedience of Adam, etc. You therefore acknowledge no original sin besides that first actual sin of Adam imputed to us, no guilt in infants besides that which exists immediately from that imputation. With what mind, then, or sense, do you call inherent corruption now simply sin, now with the epithet original sin? for so you have brought ambiguity and confusion into this your disputation, which would have been harmful to me unless I had detected it and, as I do, removed it. Here it comes upon my mind to wonder, reverend Sir, that you, when you so openly depart from the confession of our Church, could bring it into your mind to write me a great charge as if I, who religiously cling to it, had defected from it. It also grieves me that I cannot defend you, who shine before others in doctrine and holiness, and whom I love from the heart, either from inconstancy or from dissimulation: from inconstancy indeed if you have sometimes felt, sometimes not felt, that inherent corruption is truly sin, pouring forth from itself the guilt of eternal death; from dissimulation truly, if when you constantly felt it is not sin, you nevertheless in some places said and inculcated that it is sin, just as if you truly and properly believed it to be sin, and not content with that, affirmed there is no dissent between us on that matter, when it could not escape you that not only I, whom you had taken to refute, but also our Churches establish that vice formally and properly, and, as the confession of faith speaks, to be truly sin; and that those very ones who with you urge the imputation of the first sin are accustomed to divide original sin into two sins, imputed and inherent, and to attribute to each its own proper guilt of eternal death. I would praise testimonies unless the books were known to all, worn by the hands of all. Here therefore you either consent that hereditary corruption, the imputed sin of Adam being set aside, is truly sin sufficient for damning the human race, or you dissent. If you consent, revoke those reasons and solutions which in the progress of this your tractate you have built upon the contrary hypothesis. If you dissent, this will be between me and you one singular controversy, which I will most gladly undertake for defending the confession of our Churches, which seems to me most true.
pass_b_english: You add the reason: how then did death reign even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's trespass, if Adam's sin was not imputed to them? Picture a newborn, or a child dying in the womb: what in him can be called sin? His will is idle of every act and cannot sin by its own choice. He has, you will say, seeds of sin—granted—but not yet sin properly, except that origin-sin by which he sinned in Adam. So his sin is sought not in him or from himself but in the first origin, the first parent; and that sin is nothing but Adam's voluntary disobedience, and so on. You therefore own no original sin but Adam's first actual sin imputed to us, and no guilt in infants but what springs immediately from that imputation. With what mind, then, do you call inherent corruption now simply sin, now original sin? So you have poured ambiguity and confusion into your case—harmful to me had I not spotted it and, as I do, cleared it away. I wonder, reverend Sir, that you, so openly leaving our Church's confession, could charge me—who cling to it—as if I had deserted it. It also grieves me that I cannot shield you, whom I love and who outshine others in doctrine and holiness, from inconstancy or from dissimulation: inconstancy, if you have sometimes held and sometimes not held that inherent corruption is truly sin and itself yields eternal death's guilt; dissimulation, if while you steadily held it is not sin you still said and pressed in places that it is, as if you truly believed it, and even claimed we do not disagree—when you could not miss that not only I, whom you set out to refute, but our Churches too hold that vice formally and properly, and, as the confession says, truly sin; and that those who with you urge first-sin imputation usually split original sin into two—imputed and inherent—and give each its own guilt of eternal death. I would cite witnesses if the books were not known to all and worn by every hand. So either you grant that hereditary corruption, apart from Adam's imputed sin, is truly sin enough to damn the human race, or you deny it. If you grant it, take back the reasons and answers you built in this tract on the contrary premise. If you deny it, this will be our one special quarrel, which I will gladly take up to defend our Churches' confession, which seems to me most true.
source_text: Subjicis rationem: nam quinam mors regnavit tunc in eos quoque qui non peccaverunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam, si hoc peccatum Adami non fuit illis imputatum? Finge puerum recens natum vel in utero ipso matris morientem, quid in illo est quod peccatum dici possit? voluntas in ipso ab omni actione vacat, nec potest propria voluntate peccare. Habet in se, inquies, semina peccati, valeat, sed nondum peccatum proprie, nisi peccatum illud originis, quo in Adamo peccavit. Ergo peccatum illius non in ipso, vel ex seipso, sed in prima origine, id est, in primo parente quaerendum est: Nec est aliud peccatum illud quam inobedientia illa voluntaria Adami etc. Tu igitur nullum peccatum originale agnoscis praeter primum illud peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatum, nullum reatum in infantibus praeter eum qui immediate ex illa imputatione existit. Quo ergo vel animo, vel sensu, corruptionem inhaerentem modo simpliciter peccatum, modo cum epitheto peccatum originale appellas? sic enim in hanc tuam disputationem ambiguitatem et confusionem intulisti, noxiam mihi futuram nisi eam deprehendissem, ac, quod facio, sustulissem. Hic subit animum meum mirari, vir reverende, qui, cum tam aperte a confessione Ecclesiae nostrae abeas, potueris inducere in animum tuum, ut mihi, qui illi religiose adhaereo, quasi ab ea defcivissem, grandem dicam scriberes. Dolet etiam mihi quod te aliis doctrina et sanctitate praelucentem, et quem ex animo diligo, tueri non possim vel ab inconstantia, vel a dissimulatione: ab inconstantia quidem si corruptionem inhaerentem vere peccatum esse, reatum mortis aeternae ex sese fundens modo sensisti, modo non sensisti; a dissimulatione vero, si cum sentires constanter non esse peccatum, tu tamen peccatum esse aliquot locis dixisti et inculcasti, perinde ac si revera et proprie peccatum esse crederes, nec eo contentus, affirmasti inter nos ea de re nullam esse dissensionem, cum te fugere non posset, non solum me, quem refutandum sumpseras, sed Ecclesias etiam nostras vitium illud formaliter et proprie, et, ut loquitur confessio fidei, vere peccatum esse statuere; et eos ipsos, qui tecum imputationem primi peccati urgent, solitos esse peccatum originale in duo peccata dispescere, imputatum et inhaerens, ac suum utrique proprium Mortis aeternae reatum attribuere. Laudarem testimonia nisi libri omnibus noti essent, omnium triti manibus. Hic igitur aut consentis corruptionem haereditariam, seposito peccato Adami imputato, esse vere peccatum damnando generi humano sufficiens, aut dissentis. Si consentis, revoca eas rationes et solutiones, quas in progressu hujus tui tractatus contrariae hypothesi superstuxisti. Si dissentis, haec erit inter me teque unum singularis controversia, quam libentissime suscipiam pro tuenda confessione Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae mihi videtur verissima.
